Tidepool

What is it?

Tidepool is a mutual aid app designed around one premise; you shouldn't have to beg for the things you need. Imagine that I put $20 in a mailbox every week, and told all my friends, "Hey, I have $20 in my mailbox. If you need that money for anything, it's yours, just leave a note that you took it." Imagine some other neighbors did the same, everyone giving what they could spare. I want to build the app version of this.

What would stop someone from taking it all?

On a physical level, nothing. It's there in my mailbox for anyone to take. On a relational level, taking money they don't need has a cost. A large enough breach would cost them the relationships. And for many people that's too great a cost.

Has this been done before?

Yes! The ideas from this came from discussion about Peter Gelderloos's book Anarchy Works. In Chapter 2 under the heading "How will decisions be made?" He talks about communities in Spain implementing sharing amongst each other. He also discusses how these communities dealt with people trying to take advantage of this arrangement.

Gaston Leval described a general assembly in the village of Tamarite de Litera, in Huesca province, which the non-collective peasants were also allowed to attend. One problem brought up at the meeting was that several peasants who had not joined the collective left their elderly parents in the care of the collective while taking their parents’ land to farm as their own. The entire group discussed the matter, and eventually decided to adopt a specific proposal: they would not kick the elderly parents out of the collective, but they wanted to hold those peasants accountable, so they decided that the latter had to take care of their parents or else receive neither solidarity nor land from the collective.

In other words, the group worked together to hold individuals accountable. This accountability can and does happen in small groups where people aren't anonymous.

Technically what is it?

I'll sharing my full-stack android development experience in public through the next few weeks. I'll be talking about how I'm thinking about structure, scalability, usability, testing and more. I'm in my last semester of my Master's degree, so I don't expect that I'll have everything right. I'm building this in public so that I can get feedback from engineers with more experience. I'm passionate and invested in this project enough to be publicly wrong. And as a junior engineer, this project is as much about learning as it is about building something that could really help people. I'm looking forward to sharing it with you all in the next weeks!

The making of the AT Map

If you haven't seen my Appalachian Trail Map, take a look at it before reading this article

The first version of it had an inverse scrolling effect where the map in Georgia, and as the user scrolled down the map would move up. This version of the project had a couple of issues:

  • The scrolling effect was slightly jittery
  • Pictures were designed to be displayed with captions of different lengths
  • My picture / story density wasn't evenly spread throughout the trail

It was a good first attempt at a display, but ultimately, it didn't showcase all the photos I wanted, and I couldn't' find a way to fix the jittery scroll effect.

So, I went back to the drawingboard, and scrapped the scrolling effect. Instead, to address the density problem, I replaced panels on the side of the trail with dots showing exactly where the photo was taken. How is this accomplished?

The Appalachian Trail is long enough that the curvature of the earth does matter, so any simplistic solution is designed to be off by a little bit. Further, the trail actually changes every year! There's no guarantee that any particular part of the trail you see on the post is actually still apart of the trail.

Given this, we could go down the route of mapping a Mercator projection onto our map of the AT, and using that to place location from the picture's exif data. While this solution is generally applicable, there's bound to be some dots that were on trail my year, but appear off trail on the map.

To me, the effect of dots on a line is really important. To achieve I manually drew a line on top of the trail, and exported as an SVG object. Then, in the react component, we overlay the line over the map.

How do we map the coordinates to a place on the line? We do a fancy estimate. The Appalachian trail runs generally Northeast. I have pictures at the beginning and end, and can get start and end coordinates from them. From that, if we pretend that the trail is a straight line, we can get a percentage estimate by averaging the horizontal and vertical progress. Once we have the percentage, we can ask the SVG object for the point that is that percentage along.

This is a compromise, and not a perfect system. If you know what you're looking for, you can find some misplaced pictures - There's one at the bridge to Harper's Ferry that's placed nearer to Fort Royal. But it's very close, and gives the effect of being perfectly mapped.
